title: 'We're not above the law': Prince Albert police officer charged with criminal negligence in man's in-custody death
subtitle: The unnamed officer has been charged with criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessities of life in the death of 33-year-old Saul Laliberte.
article: Prince Albert's interim chief of police says the service will "trust the process" and "work with the process," after an officer was charged with criminal negligence causing death in the 2021 in-custody death of a 33-year-old man.
P.A. police say Saul Laliberte died after being taken to the service's detention facility on Nov. 7, 2021.
Following an investigation by Saskatoon police into Laliberte's death, the Crown recommended charges be laid.

The 21-year member - who was not immediately identified publicly - has been relieved of active duty, pending the outcome of court proceedings. The officer, who also faces a charge of failure to provide the necessities of life, is scheduled to appear in court on July 25.

"Although our officers on a day-to-day basis enforce the law, we know that we're not above the law and we know that we can be subjected to the law and we follow those principles," interim Chief Patrick Nogier said in an interview.

In a statement issued earlier in the day, Nogier said that while the judicial progress must be followed, the decision to relieve the officer from duty "was made with the aim of maintaining public trust."
Based on the gravity of the situation and the charges filed, Nogier said he felt that was the most appropriate course of action.
The officer will continue to be paid while the relief-from-duty order is in effect. It also means the officer is not an active member and isn't being reassigned to any administrative duties.
Nogier said he could not comment specifically on the circumstances of Laliberte's death, now that this is a criminal matter going before the court.
The president of the Prince Albert Police Association urged respect for the judicial process.

"While we firmly believe that our member acted lawfully in this specific circumstance, we understand the need for a transparent accountability process," union president Const. Nolan Carter said in a statement.

Laliberte was the third person in fewer than 30 days in the fall of 2021 to die while in custody of Prince Albert police. He had been taken to police detention on Nov. 7, 2021 after his arrest and was found unresponsive in the detention cell a few hours later.
In-detention paramedics attempted to revive him and he was taken to Victoria Hospital, where he died.

The deaths, all in separate incidents, happened shortly after the men were arrested in October and November 2021 and while they were in police custody, either at the police station or while at a hospital.

Two men died within 48 hours of each other: one, a 35-year-old man, was found unresponsive in a Prince Albert police detention cell on Oct. 11, 2021 ; and a 29-year-old man died at Victoria Hospital on Oct. 12, 2021 , after he went into what police described as "medical distress."
The province assigned an independent observer to all three investigations, while the coroner conducted separate investigations.
The deaths prompted the Prince Albert Grand Council and Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations to call on the Saskatchewan government to intervene.

In November 2022, the province called an independent review to be led by former Edmonton police chief Rod Knecht, which focused on the Prince Albert Police Service's operations. The review has not yet been publicly released.
The deaths, Nogier said, triggered an internal review of the force's policy and protocols, which are related to detention audits being conducted - but not yet completed - by the province.
They've made changes at their detention facility, including ensuring there are more robust checks and implementing an improved screening process.
The force also came under scrutiny in February 2022 for its response to a domestic violence call after a toddler in the home police attended was later found dead.

A Public Complaints Commission investigation into the initial response by police to the domestic violence report made by the boy's mother found that the two responding officers took the mother into police custody without checking on her 13-month-old son, Tanner Brass.
Tanner's father, Kaij Brass, was charged with second-degree murder in the boy's death.

The commission recommended the two officers face "appropriate discipline" for "neglect of duty" to be decided by then police chief Jonathan Bergen, who instead announced his retirement effective May 31.
